items.prompt: In a well-run dual-ladder organization, how should staff/principal engineer (IC) and engineering manager (EM) relate to each other?
choices: EM is one level above senior IC on the same ladder
They're parallel tracks, similar in pay and prestige, different in daily work
IC is a fallback for people who couldn't become managers
There's no meaningful difference between the two roles
items.explanation: A dual ladder is specifically designed so staff/principal (IC) and manager (EM) are parallel, not stacked — EM isn't a promotion above senior IC, it's a different job with comparable standing.
items.reference:
IC track

Leverage: your own technical judgment

EM track

Leverage: other people's output, multiplied

Why: above senior engineer, a well-run org runs these as two parallel tracks, not one ladder with management on top.
items.learnMore:
Two tracks, not one ladder

A dual ladder puts staff/principal engineer and engineering manager side by side, similar in pay and prestige, different in daily work. Neither sits above the other.

Common mistake

Treating EM as the promotion above senior IC. In a dual-ladder org, it's a lateral move into a different job, not a step up.

items.explanation: The three axes are energy (does the daily work energize or drain you), aptitude (real evidence you're good at it), and org need (does this org need you here specifically) — evaluated separately, not folded into one gut feeling.

items.prompt: How does this unit describe the reversibility of switching from IC to EM (or back)?
choices: Completely irreversible — once you switch, you can never switch back

items.explanation: The unit is explicit: track switches are usually reversible, but cost months of ramp-up in either direction and can affect how peers see you — a real choice, not a coin flip, but not a life sentence either.

items.learnMore:
Reversibility

Switching tracks is usually reversible, but not free: expect a real ramp-up cost in either direction, and possible shifts in how peers perceive you. Treat it as a real, weighty choice — not a permanent one, and not a trivial one either.

items.explanation: Naming the real (but non-zero) cost of reversing keeps the decision calibrated: serious enough to gather real evidence for, not so permanent-feeling that fear of an irreversible mistake distorts the choice.

items.prompt: How does this unit describe the difference between IC leverage and EM leverage?

items.explanation: The two are described as different currencies: IC leverage is direct (your own judgment applied to the work), EM leverage is indirect (decisions that let other people's output grow) — not one being a scaled-up version of the other.

IC leverage comes from your own technical judgment applied directly. EM leverage comes from decisions only a manager can make that multiply what other people produce. Neither is a smaller version of the other.

No prior evidence, discovered late

Sam had no evidence, going in, of being good at corrective conversations — unlike Priya, who got that evidence cheaply during her trial. The gap surfaced only after months at full stakes with a team of seven depending on it.

items.prompt: How does the unit frame Sam's struggles as an EM — as a personal failing, or something else?
choices: As proof Sam is a bad engineer and a bad person
As the predictable result of skipping evidence-gathering on a decision that needed all three axes, not a character flaw
As an unavoidable outcome for anyone who becomes a manager
As something that reflects poorly only on Sam's manager, never on Sam
items.explanation: The unit explicitly says none of this makes Sam a bad engineer or a bad person — it's the predictable result of skipping evidence-gathering on a decision that needed all three axes, not just org need.
items.reference: ⚙️ Predictable result of skipping evidence-gathering, not a character flaw
items.learnMore:
Not a moral failing

Sam's struggle is framed as the predictable outcome of deciding on org need alone, without a trial — not evidence Sam is a bad engineer or a bad person. Some people in Sam's position build the missing skill; others confirm, with real evidence now, that it isn't the right track. Both are legitimate.

Nothing changes either way — naming the gap has no effect
Sam must stay in the EM role regardless of outcome
items.explanation: The unit names both as legitimate: some people build the missing skill and grow into the role, others use the now-available real evidence to confirm the role isn't right for them — both are valid outcomes of assessing late rather than never.
